title: Non-decreasing Subsequences
statement:
Collect every subsequence of `nums` that has two or more elements and never goes down, meaning each element is greater than or equal to the element before it. A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more elements of `nums` while keeping the rest in their original order.

- Report each distinct sequence of values once, even if several different choices of positions produce it.
- Each subsequence lists its values in array order, but the subsequences themselves may appear in any order.
- When no such subsequence exists, return an empty list.
notes:
## Intuition

Testing all 2^n position sets and keeping the non-decreasing ones works, but equal values make many sets spell the same sequence, so a brute force needs a set of seen keys. Backtracking can avoid producing duplicates at all: build the sequence one element at a time, and at each depth try every value only once. Two branches that start the next slot with the same value would explore exactly the same futures (the later copy sees a subset of the earlier one's choices), so the first copy is enough.

## Approach

1. Keep the sequence under construction in `path` and the answers in `result`.
2. `backtrack(start)` first records a copy of `path` when it has at least two values.
3. It then makes a fresh `used` set for this depth and scans `i` from `start` to the end.
4. Skip `nums[i]` if this depth already tried that value, or if it is smaller than the last value in `path`.
5. Otherwise mark the value in `used`, push it, recurse with `i + 1`, and pop it to undo the choice.

## Example 1, step by step

With `nums = [4, 6, 7, 7]`, the first depth picks `4`. Below it, `6` gives `[4, 6]`, then `[4, 6, 7]` and `[4, 6, 7, 7]`; back at `[4, 6]` the second `7` is already in `used`, so it is skipped. Choosing `7` after `4` adds `[4, 7]` and `[4, 7, 7]`. Starting from `6` adds `[6, 7]` and `[6, 7, 7]`; starting from the first `7` adds `[7, 7]`, and the second `7` at the top depth is skipped. That is 8 sequences, the expected answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^n · n): there are at most 2^n subsequences and each one is copied in O(n).
- Space: O(n) for `path`, the recursion and the `used` sets along one branch, besides the output.

## Pitfalls

- Sorting `nums` to group duplicates (as in Subsets II) breaks the problem: the order of the original array matters.
- The `used` set must be local to each call; a global one would forbid a value from repeating, losing answers like `[7, 7]`.
- Push a copy (`[...path]`), not `path` itself, or every stored answer ends up empty after the pops.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | all distinct non-decreasing subsequences found |
| `path` | the subsequence being built |
| `start` | first index the next element may come from |
| `used` | values already tried at the current depth |
| `i` | index of the candidate next element |
